problems.title: Maximize Consecutive Elements in an Array After Modification
problems.problem: You get an array of positive integers. First you may add 1 to any elements you like (each element at most once). Then pick as many elements as possible so that, after sorting, the picked values form a run of consecutive numbers like 3,4,5 (no repeats, no gaps). Return the size of the biggest such pick.

examples.explanation: Increase index 0 (2 to 3) and index 3 (1 to 2). The array becomes [3,1,5,2,1] and we can pick 1,2,3.
Gaps are 3 apart, so even after +1 nothing can join up. Best is a single element.

problems.intuition: Every element ends up as either x or x+1. If we process numbers in sorted order, dp[v] can mean: the longest consecutive run that ends exactly at value v using elements seen so far. When we meet x, it can extend a run ending at x to end at x+1 (use it as x+1), or extend a run ending at x-1 to end at x (use it as x). Sorting guarantees every element that could come before in the run has already been processed.
approach: Sort nums.
Make an array dp sized past the max value (1000003), all zeros. dp[v] = longest run ending at value v.
For each x in sorted order: first set dp[x + 1] = dp[x] + 1 (use x as x+1), then dp[x] = dp[x - 1] + 1 (use x as x). Order matters: dp[x + 1] must read the old dp[x].
Update ans with max(dp[x], dp[x + 1]).
Return ans.
dryRun: x=5: dp[6] = 1, dp[5] = dp[4]+1 = 1, ans stays 3

complexity.space: O(M) where M is the max value (about 10^6 ints)

edgeCases: Single element: answer 1
Duplicates like [1,1]: one stays 1, one becomes 2, answer 2
Values at 10^6: x+1 = 10^6+1 still fits in the dp array
Values far apart like [1,4,7]: answer 1, while [1,3] gives 2 because 1 can become 2
problems.takeaway: When each item can take one of a few values and you want the longest consecutive chain, sort and keep dp[value] = best chain ending at that value.

problems.title: Missing Number
problems.problem: The array has n distinct numbers taken from 0..n, so exactly one number in that range is missing. Return it.

examples.explanation: n = 3, range is 0..3, and 2 is not in the array.
n = 2, range is 0..2, and 2 is not in the array.
n = 9, range is 0..9, and 8 is not in the array.

problems.intuition: XOR of a number with itself is 0 and XOR with 0 changes nothing. If we XOR every index 0..n together with every value in the array, each present number appears twice and cancels out. Only the missing number appears once, so it is what remains.
approach: Start x = n (the index n has no matching slot in the loop).
For each i from 0 to n-1, do x ^= i ^ nums[i].
Return x.
edgeCases: Missing number is n itself, like [0,1]: x keeps n
Missing number is 0, like [1,2,3]
Single element [0] gives 1 and [1] gives 0
No overflow risk, unlike the sum formula in other languages
problems.takeaway: Find the one unpaired value: XOR everything, pairs cancel. Sum formula n*(n+1)/2 minus array sum is the other classic.

problems.title: Reorder List
problems.problem: Given a singly linked list L0, L1, ..., Ln, rearrange the nodes (not the values) in place into L0, Ln, L1, Ln-1, L2, Ln-2, and so on.

examples.explanation: Take first, last, second, second last.
Same pattern, the middle node 3 ends up last.

problems.intuition: The result alternates between the front half going forward and the back half going backward. So: cut the list in the middle, reverse the second half, and then zip the two halves together one node at a time. All three steps are classic O(n), O(1) linked list moves.
approach: Find the middle with slow/fast pointers: move slow by 1 and fast by 2 while fast.next and fast.next.next exist.
Cut after slow: the second half starts at slow.next, then set slow.next = null.
Reverse the second half with prev/cur/nxt; prev ends up as its new head.
Merge: a walks the first half, b walks the reversed half. Save t1 = a.next and t2 = b.next, link a to b and b to t1, then move a = t1 and b = t2. Stop when b is null.
dryRun: fast.next = 2 and fast.next.next = 3 exist: slow = 2, fast = 3
fast.next.next is null, stop. cur = slow.next = 3, slow.next = null, first half is 1 -> 2
Reverse 3 -> 4: prev ends at 4, second half is 4 -> 3
Merge a = 1, b = 4: t1 = 2, t2 = 3, link 1 -> 4 -> 2, then a = 2, b = 3
a = 2, b = 3: t1 = null, t2 = null, link 2 -> 3 -> null, then b = null so stop
edgeCases: Single node: second half is empty, nothing changes
Two nodes: stays the same order
Odd length: the first half keeps the extra middle node so it ends up last
Duplicate values are fine because we move nodes, not values
problems.takeaway: Many linked list puzzles are just three building blocks: find middle (slow/fast), reverse, merge two lists.

problems.title: Network Delay Time
problems.problem: There are n nodes labeled 1..n and directed edges times[i] = (u, v, w) meaning a signal takes w time to go from u to v. A signal starts at node k. Return how long until every node has received it, or -1 if some node can never be reached.

examples.explanation: Node 2 reaches 1 and 3 at time 1, then 4 at time 2. The slowest node gets it at time 2.
Node 2 gets the signal at time 1.
There is no edge out of node 2, so node 1 never receives it.

problems.intuition: Each node receives the signal at its shortest path distance from k. The answer is the largest of those distances. Edge weights are non-negative, so Dijkstra works: always expand the closest unfinished node from a min-heap, and its distance is then final.
approach: Build adj: for each edge u -> v with weight w store {v, w} in adj[u].
dist[] = infinity for all, dist[k] = 0, push {k, 0} into a min-heap pq ordered by distance.
Pop {u, d}. If d > dist[u] it is a stale entry, skip it.
For each edge {v, w} of u, if d + w < dist[v], update dist[v] and push {v, dist[v]}.
When pq is empty, if any dist is still infinity return -1, otherwise return the max dist.
edgeCases: Unreachable node returns -1
Zero weight edges are fine for Dijkstra
A longer direct edge vs a shorter two hop path: dist is relaxed to the shorter one
n = 1 would give 0 since only k itself needs the signal
problems.takeaway: Single source shortest path with non-negative weights: Dijkstra with a min-heap and the skip-if-stale check. Time for everyone to receive = max of shortest distances.

problems.title: Candy
problems.problem: Children stand in a line, each with a rating. Every child gets at least one candy, and a child with a higher rating than a neighbor must get more candies than that neighbor. Return the minimum total candies.

examples.explanation: Give 1, 2, 1. The third child only needs 1 because equal ratings have no rule between them.

problems.intuition: The rule has two sides: compared with the left neighbor and with the right neighbor. Handle them separately. A left to right pass makes every increasing slope correct from the left. A right to left pass fixes decreasing slopes from the right, taking the max so we do not break what the first pass set. Each value is the smallest that satisfies both sides, so the sum is minimal.
approach: Make c with all 1s.
Left pass i = 1..n-1: if ratings[i] > ratings[i-1] then c[i] = c[i-1] + 1.
Right pass i = n-2..0: if ratings[i] > ratings[i+1] then c[i] = max(c[i], c[i+1] + 1).
Return the sum of c.
edgeCases: Single child gets 1
All equal ratings: everyone gets 1
Strictly increasing or decreasing of length n: 1+2+...+n
Peak like [1,3,4,5,2]: the max in the right pass keeps the peak big enough for both sides
problems.takeaway: When a constraint involves both neighbors, do one pass from each direction and combine with max.
